To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the scattering properties of whole blood depend on the cell shape and the cell-to-cell aggregation.
the absorption and scattering coefficients of whole blood are affected by cell shape, orientation, and aggregation.

cell shape and aggregate size have a measurable influence on the optical properties (mu(s)' and mu(a)) of blood, and that these effects can be accounted for in a simple model based on T-matrix computations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optical properties of blood cells, which is of importance for the optical evaluation of whole-blood constituents.
the optical properties of blood and blood constituents, which are important for the development of optical diagnostic tools for blood-related diseases.
the influence of cell shape and secondary, intercellular, structure on the optical properties and scattering of whole blood and red blood cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optical properties are determined by the optical properties of the single cells, though influenced to some extent by the intercellular interactions.
cell orientation, elongations and aggregate formation do influence the absorption and scattering of whole blood.
cell shape and aggregate size are not important for the optical properties of blood at the wavelengths of interest.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optical properties (mu(a), mu(s)') of whole blood are mainly determined by the properties (mu(a) (cell), mu(s) (cell)) of its individual cells.
cell morphology has an influence on the optical properties, but this influence is relatively small compared with the influence of the concentration of the cells.
the scattering coefficient of whole blood depends on the shape and orientation of the red blood cells, whereas the absorption coefficient is independent of these parameters.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cell shape and orientation have an effect on the optical properties that is not negligible, and that this effect must be taken into account if one wishes to use optical techniques to measure the properties of whole blood.

cell morphology and cell-to-cell organization influence the scattering properties of flowing whole-blood suspensions, and that the scattering properties are determined primarily by the optical properties of the individual cells, though collective scattering effects are also present.
the optical properties (absorption, reduced scattering) of blood are influenced by cell shape and aggregate structure.
